analysis.one_liner: Gives workers at larger firms up to seven paid sick days a year, usable for their own or family illness.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote; it was referred to three House committees and two subcommittees, and no chamber acted before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 15 or more employees to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours — about seven workdays — per year. Workers could use it for their own illness or medical care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, or domestic partner, or to handle medical, housing, and legal steps after domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Employers with fewer than 15 employees could opt out of paid time but would have to offer 56 hours of unpaid sick leave. The bill died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 percent of private-sector workers who lack paid sick time — disproportionately the lowest-paid workers, of whom about 70 percent have none — plus workers who have sick time they cannot use to care for a sick child or family member [S3]. Domestic violence victims would get protected time off to see doctors, move to safety, or attend court, which the bill's findings say affects a large share of employed victims and often costs them their jobs [S3]. The bill's findings cite research estimating a national policy would cut preventable emergency-room visits and save about $1.1 billion a year, including roughly $500 million for Medicaid [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Workers earn one hour of paid sick time per 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for their own health needs and to care for family members including domestic partners [S2].

Workers can use the time for medical care, relocation, counseling, or court proceedings related to domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, and employers may not retaliate against them for using it [S2].
Employers are barred from requiring workers to find their own shift replacement, counting sick time against no-fault attendance policies, or interfering with the right in any way [S3].
Workers could sue for lost wages and attorney's fees, and the Secretary of Labor would have Fair Labor Standards Act-style investigative and enforcement authority [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — especially those in low-wage, low-margin industries like retail and food service, where most workers lack sick days — pay wages for hours not worked and bear recordkeeping and enforcement exposure. Small businesses under 15 employees that opt out of paid time must still give 56 hours of unpaid leave, which means their workers lose pay when they stay home.

drawbacks.text: Covered employers bear the wage cost of sick hours and new compliance duties, a cost that falls hardest on small or low-margin businesses and can be passed to workers through reduced hours or slower raises — the bill itself frames its requirements as needing to be 'feasible for employers' [S3].

The design gives smaller employers (under 15 employees) only an unpaid-leave option, so workers at small firms would still forfeit pay to stay home sick, and the smallest workplaces — like some restaurants and domestic work — would get no paid guarantee at all [S2].
Up to 56 hours of unused time carries over year to year, which employers may see as an accumulating liability, though the bill requires no payout for unused time when a worker leaves [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is broad and direct: a guaranteed right to stay home sick without losing a paycheck, for the roughly 40 percent of private-sector workers who have none, plus protection for domestic violence victims who the record says often lose jobs over time off. The cost is a real but ordinary employer benefit cost of a capped seven days a year, and the bill limits it — no payout at separation, no replacement-worker requirement, and full credit for employers with existing policies. The unpaid-only option for the smallest employers is the weakest part of the design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee for its entire life: it was referred to three House committees and then to two subcommittees, and no committee or chamber ever voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Healthy Families Act on February 12, 2015 [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and, in addition, to the Committees on House Administration and Oversight and Government Reform [S5].
On April 29, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions — its last recorded action [S5].
It never received a hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action in the 114th Congress, which ended January 3, 2017 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that provide no paid sick time — particularly in retail and food service — kept the status quo, with no federal requirement to pay workers for days they miss due to illness. With Republicans holding the House majority and the committee chairs, the measure received no hearing or markup, so no vote was ever taken on it.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act and led the effort with 68 original cosponsors

for.name: 151 of 188 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 151 cosponsors were Democrats

against.name: John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee (R-MN), the primary committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; after subcommittee referral in April 2015 no further action occurred in two years

sides.party_line_note: All 151 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill never reached the floor of the Republican-majority House; no vote was ever taken to test support further [S4].

industries.note: These low-wage, high-turnover industries employ most of the workers without paid sick time, so they would bear the largest share of the new wage cost for sick days. The bill's absence meant their workers kept coming to work sick, which the bill's own findings link to spreading illness and injuries on the job [S3].

industries.industry: Small businesses with fewer than 15 employees
industries.note: They could opt out of paid time but would have to provide 56 hours of unpaid sick leave, a lighter burden than the paid mandate on larger firms. Their workers would still lose pay when sick, so the opt-out protects the employer's cost rather than the worker's income [S2].
Any employer whose existing policy meets the bill's amount and conditions is fully credited and need not add anything, so employers who already offer generous leave face no new cost.
The bill explicitly covers congressional staff, GAO, and Library of Congress employees under the same earned sick-time right, so Congress would have had to apply the standard to its own workforce.
